title: Systems of a Linear and a Quadratic Equation
standard_text: 2A.3C solve, algebraically, systems of two equations in two variables consisting of a linear equation and a quadratic equation; 2A.3D determine the reasonableness of solutions to systems of a linear equation and a quadratic equation in two variables
meta_desc: Free Algebra II worksheets on linear-quadratic systems for Texas TEKS 2A.3C and 2A.3D: substitution, points of intersection, number of solutions and reasonable solutions. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Set the line and the parabola equal and solve the quadratic.
body_html:
How to think about it

  • A line and a parabola can meet at 0, 1 or 2 points.
  • Substitute: set the two expressions for y equal, move every term to one side, and solve the quadratic.
  • Put each x into the line to get y. Check in both equations.
  • The discriminant b2 − 4ac tells how many: positive → 2, zero → 1, negative → 0.
  • In context, drop solutions that make no sense, like negative time.

Examples

Example

y = x2 − 2x − 1 and y = x + 3

x2 − 3x − 4 = 0

(x − 4)(x + 1) = 0

Answer: (4, 7) and (−1, 2)

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Adding the line instead of subtractingMove every term of the line to the other side.
Using the wrong yPut each x into the line or the parabola.
Keeping a negative timeTime and length cannot be negative.

faq.a: Solve, algebraically, systems of two equations in two variables consisting of a linear equation and a quadratic equation.
Determine the reasonableness of solutions to systems of a linear equation and a quadratic equation in two variables.

faq.q: Can a line touch a parabola at exactly one point?
faq.a: Yes. The line is tangent and the discriminant is 0.
No. A line and a parabola meet at most twice.
